tagline.text: The Philippines' carving capital, shaping saints and toys for over 400 years

location.label: Location
location.text: Paete, Laguna (Manila East Road, between Pakil and Pangil)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (Holy Week and the September Ukit-Taka Festival also recommended)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–2,000 (round trip from Manila, food and souvenirs, per person on a day trip)

children.text: Paete is a small town in northeastern Laguna that was proclaimed the "Carving Capital of the Philippines" in 2005. The St. James Church, the workshop streets, taka papier-mâché and the Three Crosses viewpoint can all be covered in one day, making it a good cultural day trip from Manila.
Paete is a small town of about 25,000 people in northeastern Laguna, squeezed between Laguna de Bay and the foothills of the Sierra Madre. It lies about
102km
from Manila and about
15km

from Santa Cruz, the provincial seat of Laguna. The town is said to have been founded around 1580 when Spaniards arrived with Franciscan friars, and it became an independent pueblo (San Lorenzo) in 1602. For several centuries afterward, carving saints and altars for churches was the town's main industry.

Its nickname is the "Carving Capital of the Philippines," an official title proclaimed by the president on March 15, 2005. Works by Paete craftsmen are said to be found in overseas churches such as St. Peter's Basilica in Rome and St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York. The town's honored hero is the carver Mariano Madriñan, whose "Mater Dolorosa" reportedly won a prize at an Amsterdam exhibition in 1882 and earned praise from the King of Spain. Paete people are still proud of him today.

The easiest thing for a traveler to see in Paete is the workshops and shops all over town. Saints, crucifixes, Passion scenes, furniture, decorative panels and animal carvings stand in rows, and in some shops you can watch a craftsman chiseling wood at the back. Add to this "taka," a papier-mâché craft said to have started in Paete: layers of paper are pasted over a wooden mold to make folk toys such as horses and carabaos. The town's history is not light either. On April 12, 1899, an American battalion is said to have entered Paete as part of the Laguna campaign and met strong resistance, and in 1942 Japanese troops occupied the town, with guerrilla activity continuing until Filipino and American forces liberated it in 1945. Neighboring Pakil split off as a separate town in 1676. Knowing this background makes an ordinary country town look much deeper as you walk past the church and plaza. The feast of St. James on July 25 and of St. Anthony the Abbot on January 17 bring town events, so a visit around those dates lets you see the workshops and church busy together.

It is not a famous tourist spot crowded with visitors. Instead, its charm is seeing an old craft carried on in everyday life up close. The church and plaza, a riverside cafe and the Three Crosses viewpoint on the hill can all be covered on foot and by tricycle, and the town pairs well with nearby towns such as Pagsanjan, home of Pagsanjan Falls, or Lucban in an eastern Laguna itinerary. Workshop hours and museum days change often, so check locally before you go.

Shops and workshops selling saints, crucifixes, furniture and decor line the center of town. You can step into a shop that appeals to you, watch a craftsman at work and ask about prices. Custom orders vary greatly in price with size and type of wood, so get a quote on the spot.

A Spanish-era Baroque church said to have first been built in 1646, dedicated to the town's patron saint, St. James. Inside are murals and movable statues of saints, so the town's carving tradition and faith meet in one place. Please visit quietly during Mass.

Taka is Paete's traditional folk craft of pasting paper over a wooden mold. Animal shapes such as horses and carabaos are typical, and small ones make good souvenirs. They are light but weak against moisture, so pack them carefully.

From the three crosses on the hill above town you can see the whole town and Laguna de Bay at a glance. Many people reportedly climb it as a pilgrimage during Holy Week. The path is steep with little shade, so go early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
Described as a waterfall about
high on the way to the Three Crosses. In the rainy season the water swells and is refreshing, while in the dry season the flow may shrink. The path is slippery after rain, so mind your footwear.

Known as a museum gathering the works of the carver Luis Ac-ac, and reported to be closed on Mondays. You can see how Paete's carving tradition carries into art, but opening hours need to be checked locally.

blocks.title: Wawa Park boats and lake views

children.text: At Wawa Park, small motorboats are said to take visitors out on Laguna de Bay. The view of Paete's hills from the lakeshore is quiet and relaxed.

A town festival celebrating carving (ukit) and taka, usually described as held around September. The date changes every year, so check municipal announcements. If you go then, you can see street events and exhibits.

items.title: One-day trip
items.subtitle: From Manila to carvings and the church

children.text: Take a bus from Manila (Cubao or Buendia) to Santa Cruz. Depending on traffic it takes about
2–3 hours
In Santa Cruz, transfer to a jeepney with a "Paete" or "Siniloan" signboard and ride about
15km
to Paete. To enter the town center, look for the "Paete Loob" mark.
Look around St. James the Apostle Church and the plaza. Take your time with the Baroque facade and the saints and murals inside.
Walk the workshop street and step into a few carving shops. If a craftsman is working, ask permission before watching, and compare prices for anything you like.
Have lunch near the market or at a riverside cafe. Try "bibingkang hipon," the shrimp rice cake described as a local specialty.
Take a tricycle up toward the Three Crosses viewpoint and Matabungka Falls and enjoy the lake view.
Buy taka toys and souvenirs, then head to Santa Cruz to catch a bus back to Manila.
Bus times on the return leg are irregular, so leaving Santa Cruz before 17:00 is recommended. Check the last departure locally.

items.title: Overnight trip
items.subtitle: At a relaxed pace together with eastern Laguna

children.text: Arrive in Paete in the morning, see the workshops and church, and climb to the Three Crosses in the afternoon. Eat dinner in town and stay at a nearby lodging.
Head toward neighboring Pakil and Pagsanjan to visit a waterfall or church, then return to Manila.

items.title: From Manila by bus and jeepney

children.text: Take a bus from Manila to Santa Cruz (Laguna). HM Transport at Cubao, Green Star Express on Taft Avenue, DLTB and others run this route.
In Santa Cruz, transfer to a jeepney with a "Paete" or "Siniloan" signboard. Santa Cruz to Paete is about
15km
As of 2013, the bus fare from Manila to Santa Cruz was about
. It may have risen since, so check locally.
Travel time varies greatly with Manila traffic and is described as around
2–3 hours
From Manila, take Manila East Road (via Rizal province) or the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) and then the road along Laguna de Bay. The distance is about
102km
From Santa Cruz, follow the national road through Pagsanjan, Lumban and Kalayaan. In town, turn onto J.P. Rizal Street.
The town center can be explored on foot, but many streets have no sidewalks.
Use a tricycle to reach the hilltop viewpoint or the waterfall. Fares depend on distance and bargaining, so confirm before riding.

The dry season from November to May is comfortable for walking and good for climbing to the Three Crosses and the falls. During Holy Week, religious events are held across town and it is lively but crowded.

From June to November, the rainy season, there are warnings that Manila East Road can flood from Laguna de Bay and the Paete River can swell and briefly flood the town. Postpone your trip when a typhoon is coming.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Good for walking, and the easiest time to climb to the Three Crosses.
Plan outdoor activities for early morning or late afternoon. Holy Week events also fall in this period.
Watch for road and town flooding, and check the schedule of the Ukit-Taka Festival around September.

There are not many large hotels in Paete, so most people visit as a day trip. If you need lodging, look at places in nearby Pagsanjan or Santa Cruz. Reservations and rates change by date, so check locally.

For food, bibingkang hipon, a rice cake topped with shrimp, is described as a local specialty. Around the market you can easily find Filipino home-style eateries, and a small cafe by the river is said to display local art. Opening hours of cafes and eateries need to be checked locally.
Ask permission before taking photos inside workshops. Take care not to disturb craftsmen at work.
Large carvings are hard to transport. Ask the shop whether a piece is small enough to bring on a plane and confirm how it will be packed.
Saint carvings carry religious meaning, so be polite even when bargaining over price.
There is little shade on the way up to the Three Crosses, so bring water and a hat.
To ride a jeepney into town, check that the signboard says "Paete Loob." Otherwise you must get off at the western junction and take a tricycle or walk.
Bring plenty of cash. Small shops may not accept cards.
Check the municipal office or local notices for the latest festival dates and museum hours.
In the rainy season, lake overflow and river floods can briefly submerge roads and the town. If a typhoon forecast is issued, postpone your visit.
Traffic on the way from Manila is heavy and can take longer than expected.
Many streets have no sidewalks, so watch for cars and motorcycles when walking in town.
The hill paths to the Three Crosses and the falls are slippery when it rains.
Workshop and museum closing days can change, so check before visiting.
It is not a famous tourist spot, so English guidance may be limited. Prepare a few local phrases or a translation app.
A waterfall town on the national road leading from Paete toward Manila, along the same road. It is famous for its rapids boat ride.
A traditional town in Quezon province, another cultural town of the region. It is best planned as a separate one-day trip.
A neighboring town right next to Paete, known for its Marian pilgrimage events. It is commonly combined with Paete in one itinerary.
A neighboring town farther northeast along the same Manila East Road from Paete. Its name appears together with Paete on jeepney signboards.
